utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, President. This is case IT-04-74-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say good afternoon, everybody, Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. We are going to finish our work today. Before that, I have a decision to impart to you and after that I would like the Registrar to move into private session for a couple of minutes. I will read slow so that everybody can follow. This is a verbal decision pursuant to the request of the accused Prlic concerning application for additional information regarding the confidential motion of the Prosecution requiring introduction of 11 written statements pursuant to 92 bis (A) and (B). This November, the Prosecution has filed a confidential request for admission of 11 statements. The Defence of the Accused Prlic, represented by Mr. Karnavas, required, in the name of all the accused, that the Trial Chamber grant them approval to receive additional information. The Defence claims that the Prosecution did not meet their obligation to state to what extent those written statements proposed for admission are cumulative in nature, bearing in mind that some prior witnesses have already testified to similar issues. The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution stated in their motion that the statements they propose to introduce are corroborative of prior testimony from other witnesses. The Prosecution named these witnesses. However, they failed to explain in what way these statements are cumulative relative to live testimony. We have heard the Prosecution motion does refer to a specific charge, but that is not sufficient. It is incumbent upon the Prosecution - and this is important in regard to every statement - to specify which part of viva voce testimony is corroborated by any particular statement. For that reason, the Trial Chamber shall grant the application by the Defence. And in addition to that, the time allowed to the Prosecution for making a new motion will start to run now. That means, Mr. Mundis, that you will be required to modify your motion to include the information that we have just specified. We are now going to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I was saying my name is Peter Murphy, and with my colleague, Ms. Nozica, I represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. I understand that during 1993, you spent approximately six months in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, approximately six months. Just over six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was between roughly April and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was between roughly April and November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between April and October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you left for that assignment, you received -- or during the voyage to the assignment, you received some briefing about the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We received, ever since the unit was gathered together in Almeria in Spain, we starting receiving all reports coming from the Spanish unit deployed in that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And effectively, you had to rely on that briefing for the information that you had at the beginning of your assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not only that information. Among other things, my unit had the mission of participating in conferences or lectures with the rest of the contingent. So we had to undertake a learning exercise of the whole Balkan region, the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina more concretely. In the files, all of the lectures that were given are listed to the Spanish contingent before we left into -- to go into operations, and they were geographic, historical, ethnic information included in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first time that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor about events in 1993, was that in November of 2000 when you made your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In November, 2000, I was in Kosovo, and I was called to Madrid as a witness for this court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, the Presiding Judge asked you some questions about who had initiated the conflict in the area of Jablanica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe your evidence about that was that you thought that that was the HVO who had initiated that conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he arrived and when I personally arrived in the area of operations, we had reports already about the military operations already under way in the area around Jablanica and other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also receive information that on about the 27th of March, 1993, that was before your arrival, there had been an attack by the ABiH in the area of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right now I cannot recall. We received reports of the situation throughout Bosnia and the military activities under way throughout the whole of Bosnia. It is possible, but right now, I don't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would accept, would you not, that the conflict that you became involved in in April of 1993 was very complicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because not only were there the Croats and the Muslims involved, but also the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can be permitted, that is not all there is to it, because the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina saw activities being carried out by all different parties given all of the different ethnic communities. There the Croats in the Kiseljak pocket and those in the Grude pocket didn't have the same way of going about their activities. Likewise, there were differences in the way of acting between the Muslims on the east of Mostar and the Muslims in Sarajevo or in Tuzla. And we were perfectly aware of this, and we observed it during the time that we were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we talk about one side attacking or taking the initiative, we have to bear in mind that different parties were attacking at different times and at different places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but I repeat that the first question you asked me was about the operations, the military operations, close to Jablanica and in Doljani, Sovici, Slatina. In these communities, when we arrived, the news that we had was that the HVO forces were completing military operations there and that they were cleansing the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would agree, would you not, as a professional soldier, that when you had military action in one area, it can spill over; the consequences of that then lead on to an action in an area close by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I wanted to point out that, as a professional soldier, from the start I realised, as did my companions, that the military actions under way in many cases were not following military -- logical military doctrine. Rather, they were being carried out in a -- in an amateur way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was quite chaotic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the symptoms of that, as you mentioned yesterday, was that the commanders could not always compel their subordinates to carry out orders that they gave, for example, that cease-fires should be observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some or many cases this is the case. But I would like to point out, that in many cases, the failure to complete higher commands was not actually apparent to us. We didn't know whether this failure to fulfil orders was because of a lack of will on the part of the medium-level local command or whether these same people were receiving records along these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also observed, on the ground, that there were some units from all the parties which, if I can put it this way, were simply out of control, in the sense that they did not appear to respect any chain of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, theoretically, on paper, there was a chain of command. In practice, from our point of view, as UNPROFOR soldiers, the agreements that had reached a certain level were not implemented at the lower levels. I repeat that we were not aware whether this was because of ignorance on the local medium-level commandment level or whether once the agreement had been signed, different orders had been issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did observe, did you not, though, that on the ground there were certain elements that would take action into their own hands, for whatever reason that might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat, acting on their own initiative, I would not dare to go so far as to say that. Theoretically, there was a chain of command which was clearly defined. There was a series of units which had a less clear chain of command. I could name, for example, in the Croatian defence forces, the case of an interlocutor with which we had conversations frequently, which was Mr. Andabak. According to him, he was commander of the special operations, and sometimes he told us that he depended on the commander in chief of the Croatian defence forces, and other times he told us he followed orders coming from President Boban himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because we don't have much time, I want to move this along if I can, Witness. May we have on e-court, please, Prosecution Exhibit number 1717. And while that's coming up, Witness, what I'm going to show you is the operations logbook of the unit to which you were attached. Are you familiar with that document? You will be able to see it on the screen, Witness. I understand that you do read English quite well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have any difficulty, though, please let me know. May we see page 53 of this document, please, in English. Do you have the English version on the screen? Yes, please. What I'm going to show you, sir, is an entry for the 4th of May, 1993. And to save time, while it's coming up on the screen, if I may, I will read a short passage of this to you. It describes an occasion when an escort from your unit was providing transportation and protection for General Halilovic and General Pasalic after a meeting, and there was a reference to -- that during the trip, various groups of out-of-control-armija elements obstructed the passage of the escorts. Do you recall an incident like that? It's on the screen. It's the 5th of May, so if we could go back a bit, please, to the 4th of May. Do you recall an incident, Witness, of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. I was part of the column heading towards Doljani and Sovici, and the other part the column with General Petkovic was heading towards Konjic. In Konjic, the convoy was stopped by ABiH local forces who maintained that the UNPROFOR soldiers should hand in General Petkovic as a prisoner of war. We refused --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you, but my own question was -- since we're short of time, I just wanted to get your recollection. And then following on immediately after that on the same page, there's a reference to a lieutenant. I won't mention his name, but another officer in your company being surrounded by forces of the armija and trying to compel the joint commission to -- to go to Konjic. You remember that incident also? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I remember that this was resolved with General Halilovic's involvement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... same exhibit to page 103, please. And you'll see there an entry for the 28th of June, 1993, which reflects that on that day at about 1.30, 13.30, a team from the European Community was detained by some people called Mujahedin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's not on the screen yet, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just ask you then. We should be looking -- I'm sorry, the date should be the 28th of June. It's page 103. But let me -- let me just ask you generally, without reference to the document. Do you recall an occasion when representatives from the European Community were surrounded and detained by people who were described as Mujahedin on or about the 28th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember hearing about the presence of Mujahedin fighters or so-called Mujahedin in the northern area of Jablanica; more concretely, in the mosque of Sovici. This information, after having reading Kiseljak reports on the possible presence of these irregular fighters, we heard from a commander of the ABiH forces, Haso Hakalovic, and we had good relations with him and he confirmed the presence of the Mujahedin fighters in this mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one other point on that general subject. In your statement to the -- your witness statement to the Prosecutor, you also referred to having seen on one occasion some Croat combatants who were wearing black shirts with the symbol of the black eagle. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That was when, more precisely, on that particular day of the visits to the areas in conflict, the column was visiting at Doljani, Sovici, there were elements of the Croatian defence forces wearing this black shirt underneath their other uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other matter on that general subject. It's also true, is it not, that all the parties to the conflict made use of snipers during the time while you were in theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your professional activities, you were very much concerned with convoys of humanitarian aid, were you not? That was one of the main purposes of your activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in the area, that was our sole mission, to guarantee humanitarian aid flows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were occasions, were there not, sir, when abuses were made of such convoys because weapons were found concealed in what were, on the face of it, humanitarian supplies? Do you remember incidents of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard and we received reports to the effect, that in one truck, which was part of humanitarian aid convoy, had war materiel in it. I believe that this was outside of our area of operations. Therefore, from that time on, an order was issued so that our Ploce liaison officer, whenever there was a truck, he would make a detailed inventory of all the cargo of each truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that occasion that you just referred to, was that a convoy for which the -- the UNHCR was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNHCR was in charge of all of the humanitarian aid dispatch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were smaller humanitarian organisations that also operated in your area of responsibility, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there were other organisations, non-governmental organisations, but all of them -- and here I would have to explain the concept of a lead agency, the leader agency. One of the UN-named agent -- a leader agency to coordinate all of the activities of all the other agencies working in that area. In this case, the leader agency was part of the UNHCR anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put this question: Is it not true, sir, that there were a number of occasions during the months when you were in theatre when weapons were found concealed in different convoys? A number of separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I only recall the one that I mentioned, and I repeat that these were reports that we received in our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If you would just allow me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much. Your Honour, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon to you. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I am an attorney from Zagreb. Here with me is Mr. Stewart, a lawyer from London. We are the Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic, and we have an hour at our disposal, thanks to the Trial Chamber and my colleagues Mr. Karnavas and Mr. Ibrisimovic for giving us the time. I'm going to start off by asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment counsel. You have one hour. Explain that to me. 30 minutes plus 15 minutes from Mr. Karnavas; is that right? And another 15 minutes from whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A few questions about Jablanica. In response to a question from His Honour Judge Antonetti and now from Mr. Murphy, you spoke of the activities of the HVO in the general area of Jablanica. What I'm interested in is the following: It is not the area of Jablanica itself but the town of Jablanica. So to start off with, I'm going to ask you this: In preparing for testimony at this Tribunal, did you have an opportunity of looking through all the reports of the Spanish Battalion prepared for this trial by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to point one thing out. During my time in the area of operations, I wasn't only in Jablanica. I was all around the area of operations from Mitrovic in the south to Sarajevo in the north. During my time in Jablanica, every day I went out of the detachment and the town of Jablanica to see other places and to visit commandments throughout the area. We were not hermits in our command in Jablanica. Indeed, in preparing for this trial, the Prosecutor provided me with a number of reports relating to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I'm going to ask you about the offensive activities that you referred to in the Jablanica area, and within that framework, I'm going to ask you about what had to do with the town of Jablanica itself. So I'm not going to ask you about Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina, but the activities that were geared towards Jablanica. If necessary, I can explain the reasons for that. But tell us, please, to begin with, whether you know what was happening in the area of the neighbouring municipality such as Konjic municipality when the combat was taking place in the Jablanica area, that is to say Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina? Do you know what was happening in Konjic and the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed as to what was happening throughout the area of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Konjic, how far is that from Jablanica? How many kilometres approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about 20 minutes by road, but I don't have the exact distances in my memory right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pusic has just told us that it is 20 kilometres, if that is important to the Trial Chamber. That will be of assistance, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you spoke about the offensive actions by the HVO in the Jablanica area, did that refer to some offensive action towards the town of Jablanica itself with the intention of taking control of the town, of expelling the Muslims, and having the Croats control the town so that the town, as ethnically pure, could be integrated into the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Jablanica, especially in the north of Jablanica, there were military operations on a widespread scale. Given the reports that we received from the area of Prozor, the Croatian defence forces were putting pressure on -- towards Jablanica. Similarly, in the areas around Konjic, the ABiH forces were trying to take the small towns nearby or near Konjic. I remember Radesine, for example, in which the Croatian population was expelled by the ABiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in what you've just said, this pressure against Jablanica from the direction of Prozor and the west. This assessment of yours that it was pressure on Jablanica, did that mean that that was the objective of the HVO, to exert pressure on Jablanica? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see the HVO operation's plans. I cannot say what their intention was. What I can say is what the result of these operations was. The result of the operations was that in the town of Jablanica many refugees started to arrive. They were civilians who had been displaced from municipalities which were Muslim in their majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your military experience, refugees from one area are pouring into a town which was shelled heavily on a daily basis, which was under siege by an enemy army, and which the enemy army wanted to expel the population from, that is to take control and expel the population who were of a different ethnic group. In your experience, was that something that could happen? Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my experience, not only is it possible, it is actually what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether any report by SpaBat, and you had a chance to look through the reports in preparing for your testimony, was there a single report by SpaBat where it stated that the HVO intended to take control of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right now I cannot recall whether -- whether this is stated in any document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Defence counsel has been asking some very interesting questions, and one of those with military -- was with military overtones, but you didn't answer the question, I don't think. What she was asking you -- well, she asked you what you did, and you said that there was pressure from the HVO towards Jablanica, on Jablanica. That's the first thing. The second element is this: You said that there were refugees who arrived in Jablanica. And the third element is this: You said that the HVO launched an offensive on Jablanica. So we can see the scenario. Now, quite rightly, the Defence counsel was asking you, in this type of scenario, with this type of scenario, how is it that you, the international specialists who were on the ground, did not send out this information in a report, did not reflect all these things that could have had a logic of their own in your reports? So that is the question, and that's the question that I wanted to ask you, and can you answer that? The scenario as has just been described to us, was it ever contained and reflected and described in a report by the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember if precisely in those words this is stated, whether there is a report of this nature among those which I looked at. My personal impression from these operations, the Neretva River is very important from a strategic point of view given -- because of the hydroelectric power. Production of hydroelectric power from the Neretva River is enough to power all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there is even enough to export. Controlling the dams all along the river is vital for controlling hydroelectric power generation. The biggest power station is in Jablanica. Logically, or from a military point of view, taking Jablanica is very important from a strategic point of view, given the energy factor on the one hand and also because it is a vital crossroads for connecting the south of Herzegovina with Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is not the largest hydroelectric power plant on the Neretva, the one in Jablanica, but we can discuss that in due course. But I'd now like to go through the documents of the Spanish Battalion, and from the documents provided by your battalion, it would emerge that the HVO did not have the intention of taking control of the town of Jablanica, although, without a doubt, there was combat in the area of Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina. And I'd just like to mention that the Prosecution did not provide us with a Spanish Battalion report for the 15th of April, 1993. So the first -- next document is the 16th of April. So may we have on e-court document P 01914. Witness, if you're looking at the English text, we have prepared a set of documents for you in English which we intend to use during your testimony. And this document is one that states what happened in the Jablanica area. And at the beginning of that document, you can see that there is not a single word saying that on that day Jablanica was shelled. On page 2 of the text, it is said, "During yesterday's shelling, 32 civilians took refuge in the base and the convoy of the main command of the BH army." Now, tell us, please, Witness, on the 16th of April, if there was an HVO offensive against the town of Jablanica, wouldn't that certainly have been reflected and recorded in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document. I ought to remind you that for the preparation of my -- my presence here in this court, I understand that two paragraphs above it can be read that the authorities of the armija feared that the Croatian defence forces might be able to take advantage of the movement of the convoys and approach and bring military weapons and personnel towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In any case, not to look at the references in the text, I'd just like to emphasise that this is the document as we have it in the B/C/S and in English, and it was provided by the Prosecution. You have not seen it because the Prosecution did not intend to introduce the document through you, but there is no mention about -- of any HVO offensive. That's certain. Now I'd like to take a look at the next document, and I'd like the usher or registrar to put it on e-court. P 01964 is the document number. And while we're waiting for the document to appear on our screens, I'd like to give an explanation. The title of the document -- or, rather, on the title page, the date is the 14th of April, 1993. However, it is in fact a document which was compiled in Madrid on the 16th of April, 1993, and that can be seen from the last page of the document. And we are, of course, interested in the Jablanica area and the 15th of April, which is to be found in point 1.3 of the document. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to remind the counsel that the witness arrived in the area of Jablanica on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that the witness arrived in the area of Jablanica after these events, but the witness himself emphasised, and my learned friends from the Prosecution stressed it themselves in the examination-in-chief, that he had received -- he had been receiving for a while, before his arrival, daily reports on developments of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is relevant to adjudicated fact number 30, which refers to the alleged operation to capture Jablanica, which would then also be the context of the ultimatum of the 19th of April, the conduct of the -- sorry, 15th of April, the conduct of the offensive, et cetera. That is the context of my question. So the document I mentioned, in item 1.3, we read: "In the last few days, the tensions between Muslims and Croats have increased again. One of the elements -- one of the contributing elements was the appointment of a Muslim mayor, a radical, who was elected by the Presidency for towns of Jablanica and Konjic." And, which is important to us: "In the morning of the 15th of April, HVO pulled out the headquarters of the battalion from the town of Jablanica, relocating it."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Witness, did you see this report before arriving in Bosnia? Were you informed that the developments followed the course described in this paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed and I received this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I would like to make one point. The Prosecution did not disclose to us at all the reports of the Spanish Battalion for the period of 17th through the 20th of April. The first one we have is for the 21st of April in this set of documents. P 02008. On page 3 of that document, which regards Jablanica, under subtitle "Shelling," there is not a single word. So we would appreciate it if you would explain, Witness. When in your report, under sub-heading "Shelling", there are no specific descriptions, that means that there was no shelling. Isn't that so? Is that correct? Is that how we are to understand your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. If there is no list or no comment in that particular sub-heading, it's because we have no relevant information to put there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let us look at the Prosecution's set of documents. 02011, also the segment concerning Jablanica. In paragraph 1 we read that: "The main concern for BH forces is the situation in Doljani and Sovici." It is reasonable to interpret this as meaning that the situation in Jablanica is no reason for concern. It does not give rise to anxiety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am waiting to see the report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So again, this is document P 02011, page 3. In B/C/S version, it's page 3. Unfortunately, I do not have Spanish documents, and I cannot give you a reference, but I did read out the sentence. It reads verbatim: "The main concern for BH forces is the situation in Doljani and Sovici." Very well. In order not to waste too much time, could we please look at the general assessment in this document. We will move to another document, because the English and other versions of this particular one are not quite consistent. The next one is P 02185. This is a document in which, again, in the segment regarding the situation in the Neretva valley, it's paragraph 1, Neretva valley, we'll find this sentence -- Witness, I would be grateful if you could focus on my words and what I say, because matters are very simple here. So in the report we read: "On the 19th, another meeting was held in the staff of the battalion in Medjugorje presided by General Morillon. He took note of the request of the chief observer, General Pellnas, and decided that on the next day, the 20th of April, at 10.00 a.m., Spanish units would be deployed in places where conflicts are ongoing. Konjic, Parsovici and Mostar." What I would like to emphasise is that Jablanica is not mentioned among these places where conflicts are ongoing. Is my conclusion correct? Could you just say it aloud so we have it on record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your conclusion is correct, but there is an error. In Jablanica, we did didn't require a deployment of our unit because, within the population itself, there was our detachment which was garrisoned throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But it was also deployed in Mostar, and still you mention Mostar. You had been stationed in Medjugorje? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just say one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] In the report that my counsel is reading, that they were deployed in Parsovici, Mostar, Konjic, we read the next sentence saying: "Units of the HVO allegedly attacked Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina villages." I think that many others from the UNPROFOR would have noted if we had attacked Jablanica. If we had really attacked it, it would have been reflected in other documents. However, it isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seem to recall, and if I have used the words "attack on Jablanica," maybe it has been misunderstood. The attacks that were orchestrated in Doljani, Sovici, and Slatina followed a single line. They were all along one axis. What I meant was that an attack was being carried out moving towards Jablanica. In Jablanica, in the months, mainly, let's say the end of April, May, June, and July, Jablanica was heavily shelled during that time. The shelling was -- this shelling period was when our forces tried to protect any areas that were likely to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, would it have been logical to attack Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina without attacking Jablanica? If you, as the head of the Spanish Battalion, had to conduct such a military operation, would you have attacked these villages while leaving Jablanica alone, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In military terms, strictly attacking the villages of Doljani, Sovici, and Slatina is a stepping-stone, a necessary prerequisite to attacking Jablanica. What would not be logical, Your Honour, would be to attack these communities because, in a military point of view, they have no consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just thought of another question. The Spanish Battalion realises that Doljani, Sovici, and Slatina are attacked. In military terms, you just explained, that logic requires that Jablanica be attacked too. We know that there are units of the Spanish Battalion in Jablanica. Now, at this moment, would there be measures taken at the level of the battalion at least to protect yourselves? So were measures taken at the level of the battalion to protect your own troops? There is an attack going on. You are telling yourself there is a risk to the town. Would it have been reasonable to leave the town or take some other steps in conformity with the rules of engagement? What would have been your reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. The Spanish detachment in Jablanica, all along this time, was carrying out strengthening tasks. Subterranean shelters were built, and furthermore, all buildings were protected with sandbags. As for the detachment itself and the security of the forces themselves. Now, as for the people of Jablanica, we had talks with the authorities and it was the authorities themselves that were responsible for preparing the city militarily, and that did not involve our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now kindly ask you for leave for my client to ask this witness about another alternative explanation of this military action against Sovici, Doljani, and Slatina that would exclude the intention to attack Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all, I would like to come back to this document. On the 19th, you really did come out into those places quoted here, Konjic, Parsovici and Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General, are we talking about May? No. April?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th April. On the 20th April, there was a change of authority. So after this date, yes, I did go to Konjic and Jablanica. In the first week of our stay in the operational area, we did a reconnaissance activity, and during that, if -- if my memory serves --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I know all that. Let us go back to the area of Jablanica and Konjic. Please, on the 19th, in my presence, you received orders from General Morillon to pull out your forces into Parsovici and the broader area of Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, at the meeting, during the agreement chaired by General Pellnas, there was a signatory, and as a result of this agreement, our orders were to send patrol so that our presence is seen in the entire area, and that is how we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient for me. Please, from Jablanica you sent out patrols to Konjic and Parsovici. We know that Konjic belongs to Konjic municipality. To which municipality did Parsovici belong? Did Parsovici also fall into the Konjic municipality? Do you know whether they are on the opposite side of Konjic? As soon as you pass Ostrozac it's across the road. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this moment, I don't know exactly what Parsovici's situation was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suppose that you visited Haso Hakalovic at least once in the command. I suppose you know who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. More than once. But you and the Tribunal have to understand the problem of the names. I'm referring to the names of the population -- of the towns. If Parsovici is the place where Haso had its headquarters at that time, yes, I did go to that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we just concluded Konjic, the broader area of Konjic. And Parsovici are also integral parts of Konjic municipality. The negotiators and people leading the meeting make a decision for UNPROFOR to leave the municipality of Konjic. Is that what we can see from this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it exactly the opposite way. In that agreement, the decision was made to establish patrols in the entire area, in all this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can just say that the interpretation is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic is asking you very precisely. Following that meeting attended by General Morillon, General Petkovic as well, there was an agreement reached. According to that agreement, UNPROFOR had to leave Konjic. That's the thesis of General Petkovic. It seems that you are saying no, that what was agreed was that UNPROFOR was to send out patrols into the area. Therefore, how do you remember that agreement? Because it seems that you and General Petkovic do not agree on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's precisely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a misinterpretation, and that's what I wanted to say. My client asked a question saying that UNPROFOR was supposed to go to Konjic rather than away from Konjic, so that the witness answered at cross-purposes at first. His answer actually is on the same line as the question of my client. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat. From your base in Jablanica, your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. It seems the French interpreters are asleep because we have no more interpretation. Very well. They woke up. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: May we conclude, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I have to say in the defence of the interpreters that it is very difficult when almost three of you speak at the same time. So it is that I would like to emphasise. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, on the 20th, with one of your patrols, you set out towards Doljani. Do you remember that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember. On the 20th April, 1993, I don't remember having gone to Doljani on that day, to Doljani. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: One of your patrols took off together with a mixed commission to Doljani. Did you read that in your report if you weren't there? That's P 02012.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was when two patrols were organised, one for Doljani-Sovici, and the other one for Konjic, and that is when this incident in Konjic took place, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would conclude this: It's not without reason that UNPROFOR sent patrols that evening to the area of Konjic municipality in addition to Sovici and Doljani. Right, or not? They had reason to send them. You are nodding. You have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were reasons for sending patrols.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that the first meeting was held on the 18th. General Morillon arrived on the 19th and the patrol was sent out. Do you remember that the fighting in Sovici and Doljani had stopped and your patrol arrived on the 20th in Doljani and there was no fighting? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Military action had been concluded. The towns were empty, and what we observed was the result of the actions that were carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doljani is a village, not a town. Six hundred inhabitants is not a town by our standards; it's a village. Now, a military question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to intervene on the linguistic point. In the English language, one does refer to town where we would say village. So it's a linguistic thing. There's no difference. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. We who are from a village get upset when they tell us we are from a town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we see from this that fighting takes place in Konjic simultaneously as in the area of Jablanica. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were confrontations all over the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you stated that you were not there in end March and early April, and that you do not know what the situation was in the area of Konjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's not the witness's allegation that he didn't know. On the contrary, he stated that by the time he got some information of what was happening in the area. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it militarily justified in order to assist the HVO Brigade of Herceg Stjepan in Konjic. You know about the Konjic pocket and about Kostajnica, and because it was impossible to get there and link up with forces in Kostajnica, to exert pressure on another part of the front line in order to cause at best a cessation of talks and negotiations, could that be one of the justifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be. I must repeat that I did not see the plans of the Croatian defence forces. I don't know what the intention was behind these attacks, but from a military point of view, there is a logic no it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. You are also a witness of those events. The attack on Sovici began on the 17th, and the orders to stop fighting arrived on the 18th from the highest level, and the whole machinery of the international community was set in motion, together with the commanders of the HVO. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th was the date when we had the meeting, and the 19th was when General Morillon gave the order to form these patrols.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true, but on the 17th, according to all the witness statements and according to the Prosecution, they say that Sovici was attacked by the HVO, and on the 18th, the order came from the top-most level to cease-fire in Sovici, Doljani, and also Konjic, Kostajnica, and the town of Konjic itself. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when the Croatian defence forces gave the order to stop the operations. What is true is that when the patrol went into that area, military operations had stopped. It's also true that there is no civilian population left in those -- in that area except for those that were held in the Sovici school.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for now. I'll hand the examination over to my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I know how much more time I have for the defence of General Petkovic to be able to organise myself during the break?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been informed that you've already used 30 minutes, which means you have another 30 minutes. So the best thing to do is to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at five minutes past 4.00 and then you'll have 30 minutes running from that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Just a moment, please, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to you. We have been -- I don't know whether this is working. It is burning, but it's not working. Does the microphone -- okay. We've been talking about military logic, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Or explain to us any military logic in attacking the valley of Sovici and Doljani and then driving away or imprisoning all the Muslims but not the Croats. Can there be any military logic behind such a tactic, if one can call it like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could explain, Your Honour, the military logic on the movements within that territory. The valley in which these towns, Doljani and Sovici, are located, are what we military personnel call an area of approximation, which means on the way to Jablanica. That's why I stated that from a military logical point of view, if an operation is launched to take Jablanica, taking and occupying these towns is a vital step. I hope that with this I have answered your question. The treatment of civilians in these towns is not part of the military logic. Normally, when a military unit launches an operation, it tries to cause as little damage as possible to the civilian population. So within the military logic, the idea of removing the civilian population to avoid any damage to this population is possible. Thank you. Your Honour, I would like to clarify one issue from the previous session. We talked about visits made by Spanish troops to these towns, Doljani and Sovici. Indeed, a visit was undertaken on the 20th of April by a Spanish patrol. Quite honestly, I must state that I do not recall whether I take part personally in this patrol or not. Later, on the 4th of May, as result of another agreement, a second visit was carried out, and there I remember perfectly that I did take part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, to follow on from what you said, it seems that after the agreements, you said that you went to Sovici with General Petkovic. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the visit undertaken on the 4th of May, I went accompanying General Halilovic to the towns of Doljani, Sovici, and later Sivnica and Velici. In the visit of the 20th of April, I do not remember, and I must apologise for this, but I really am not capable of stipulating whether or not I took part in that patrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving us that additional explanation. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I apologise for that rather abrupt form of address but you know the reasons. The -- you arrived in Medjugorje on the 19th of April. Did you go straight into work that same evening in some way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then so far as the next period is concerned and the documentation, can we take it that you have not, for example, read the complete run of intelligence reports for April and May but only the particular ones that were selected for presentation to you for the preparation of your evidence here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the mission, I read on a daily basis all the reports, and in the case of most of them, it was myself, I myself, who drafted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll stop you, Witness, because we're at cross-purposes. I'm not questioning that you read the stuff scrupulously at the time you were in the region. My -- I was asking you whether it was correct that this year, I assume it's this year, for the purposes of your evidence here, you only read the selected batch of material presented to you and not, for example, the whole run of intelligence reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. This year I read the material that the Prosecutor provided me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you very fairly said in the correction you've offered since the break, that you don't remember whether you took part in that visit to Doljani and so on on the 20th of April. Is it also correct, because you were asked yesterday by His Honour Judge Trechsel whether you could confirm that the first time you were in Jablanica was before the 21st of April, which must mean on the 20th. Is it also correct that you can't, in fact, now remember whether you did go to Jablanica on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited the area of Jablanica-Konjic, and, in particular, the detachment of Spanish troops in Jablanica during my first week in the area. If I took part, precisely, in the patrol, which on the 20th of April visited Doljani and Sovici, I'm afraid I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, we seem to be moving quite close together, Witness. The position is you simply can't say now for sure whether you were or weren't in Jablanica before the 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. Excuse me. In Jablanica, yes. Yes, I did take part in the patrol that we have mentioned which was carrying out reconnaissance tasks. It's Doljani and Sovici that I can't confirm. In the week from the 20th to the 25th, I know that I did visit these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this was part of what you described in your evidence as your reconnaissance. This was your -- well, necessary familiarisation with your area of responsibility, well, just to see the lie of the land; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so far as Doljani and Sovici were concerned, I think you have said yourself today that -- and it was mentioned that by the time we got to the 17th of April, before you'd even arrived in Croatia, the main conflict had started and finished, and you read that in the reports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In the intelligence reports that we had received in Spanish territory, there was a mention of this conflict in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings yourself, and I'm talking but you personally now, just to draw the distinction between you and your group and your colleagues, did you have any dealings yourself with somebody known as Tuta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I never met with the man known by the name as Tuta. Yes, I -- I did have many meetings with Mr. Ivan Andabak, which according to him, was the lieutenant of a so-called Tuta person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was the man who spoke good Spanish; is that right? Presumably that was one good reason why you tended to meet him quite often; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not Tuta, no. Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, understood. Understood. I hope everybody understood. I understood you weren't talking about Tuta. You were talking about the other gentleman, Ivan Andabak. So far as Tuta is concerned, you know -- you know his real name, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Tuta was a pseudonym. I know what Tuta means. And right now I cannot recall his real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's speed it up then. He's Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we know who we're talking about even if I'm struggling with the pronunciation immediately. And what did you know -- immediately after your arrival in Croatia, what did you know about his role -- well, I'm sorry, in Croatia, and then on into Bosnia, what did you know about his activities and his role in the events in Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had reports which indicated that the head of the operations of the Croatian Defence Council in the area of Doljani and Sovici was this person Tuta.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you know of somebody who was -- went under the name or nickname of Cikota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That doesn't ring a bell, Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to see whether it does jog any memory or ring any bell, Cikota who was one of Tuta's men, one of Tuta's associates, and was killed. Does that ring any bells or jog any memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you read or hear reports after that -- that main fighting which we've agreed started and finished by the 17th of April, did you read and hear reports of quite serious actions taken in Doljani and Sovici over the next few days, burning of houses and so on? Did those come to your ears or to your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember reading reports relating to the situation and of what little we could see or what our forces could see. There was mention of expulsion of civilians and the burning of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it understood by you is that Tuta had a significant role in such reported events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reports that we had told us that Tuta was in charge of the operations on the Croatian Defence Council side in that area. On the other hand, we had reports on these serious activities, and that's all I'm able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear or read of any suggestion that Tuta had his own special motives involving some type of revenge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall having heard or read anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on then to -- now, Mr. Petkovic, yesterday, you heard, said that it was the 3rd of May that you first came to Jablanica. So we're leaving aside the sort of reconnaissance exercise which you'd mentioned earlier about which we're not disagreeing, but -- so when we're talking about a specific visit, you'd agree with what Mr. Petkovic says about that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seem to recall that it was the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll go with the 4th of May, and we won't have a big dispute about that, Witness. And do you recall, then, that on that visit there was an agreement reached between Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic that civilians should be moved to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember this element of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic had any private discussion either -- well, first of all, private discussion not in your presence on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. On the day, and I think it was the 4th of May, or it might have been the 3rd of May when that Jablanica meeting was held, once the agreement was completed, I don't remember exactly upon the initiative of whom, but I do recall that General Petkovic and General Halilovic did request that we give them leave to have a private discussion. We provided them with one of our Spanish detachment's offices, and there we let them talk together in private for a few minutes. We did not know what the conversation was about because obviously we were not present in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you said that you gave them leave to have a private discussion, who was in charge? Whose decision was it to give them leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that we were within the Spanish detachment and that the meeting was attended by the head of the Spanish Battalion, it was -- it was colonel in charge of the Spanish Battalion himself who gave the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was your superior, your colonel. And may it be shown, please, the document which is P 02203. I think since you read and handle English with facility, Witness, that's the one clearly to give you. Do you have that? It's quite a short document, and it has, do you see, Mr. Petkovic's name at the bottom. It's got some illegible words, apparently, though from our checking, it should and can read "Did five buses arrive in Sovici or Doljani?" We had a look at the text in the B/C/S version, "to evacuate the population (Greens) towards Jablanica? If so, where did they come from," and then apparently the word "buses" appears we think in the B/C/S version. Now, do you know -- if you don't, say so. Do you know that Mr. Petkovic did not actually write this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you -- well, first of all, do you know yourself where Mr. Petkovic was on the 5th of May, which is the date of this document? Again, if you don't know, say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. On the 4th of May, when the visit of the region was concluded, General Petkovic was transferred by Spanish Battalion vehicles to Mostar. And if my memory serves me correctly, he left the Spanish Battalion vehicles in the headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, again, it's a slightly different question, but again if you don't know -- do you know that Mr. Petkovic was not in Mostar on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to just show you a series of agreements, just to see whether you can give any personal firsthand input into these particular items. The first one is -- the number is 2D 00089, and it's a document dated the 18th of April. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. Well -- it's got another number which may help. 3D 00559, in case that makes it any easier for anybody to produce it. I can't offer any more than that, those two numbers. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. You see it's described as "Joint declaration." I'm looking at the annex signed -- it shows at the bottom by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban, a joint declaration by the president of the Republic of Bosnia and the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And the key point is item 3. I'm obviously happy to go through anything else if anyone thinks I'm skipping over something absolutely vital, but the result is: "3, We order all units to cease hostilities immediately, release prisoners and, through negotiation at all levels, remove the causes of conflict." Now, you weren't there on the 18th of April or indeed perhaps not at all in Zagreb, but this was a document that you were more or less immediately familiarised with, was it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, honestly speaking, I can't remember seeing this document till today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's a very fair answer, then, Witness. The next document, then, which is really a follow-up for that. The number for that one is P 1959. If you've got this bundle of paper documents as well, you'll find it in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Stewart. The document that we've already seen, 3D 00559, I'd like to make two observations about it. First of all, I can see on that document that there is departure from Zagreb on the 18th of April at 10.50 hours. So this seems to be a faxed document. That's what we have at the top. My second observation is that the signature of Izetbegovic should be compared to other signatures of Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not for one moment questioning that. I think Your Honour has a different physical version of this document from the one I've got. But may I just say, that in light of the witness's answer, perhaps such issues could be explored some other time, because the witness has said he don't remember seeing this document at all, so perhaps questions about its -- its signature can just be put on one side for the moment, with respect. Or, well, perhaps they don't [Microphone not activated] Ms. Alaburic has got something to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we wish to compare various signatures of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, I suggest we look among others. Document P 02088, which is a joint statement of the 24th or the 25th of April, 1993. We can compare these signatures to others we have seen. I don't think this is in dispute, because that's the document on the basis of which both Mr. Arif Pasalic and Mr. Izetbegovic issued certain orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Perhaps my wish to speed on is because I'm never quite sure whose time such things count as. So can we then look at P 1959, Witness, which is a document dated also 18th April with the name Petkovic, Milivoj Petkovic at the bottom. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And the first paragraph, the body of it says: "On the basis of the conclusions reached after the talks between Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, which took place on 18th of April, 1993, in Zagreb, and in accordance with point 3 of the agreement," which at least appears to match the point which I drew attention to, "I hereby order that: 1, All HVO units shall immediately cease hostilities with BH army units," and then 2 refers to exchange of prisoners, 3 care for wounded, and "4, reliable information shall be gathered concerning the protagonists of the conflict, the expulsion of the civilian population, the killing of captured soldiers and civilians, the torching of houses -- of the houses and other buildings." And then contact was to be established with the BH army command. And I would just like, please, before asking that -- the question about that to let you see what's a sister document or, perhaps, it's a brother document to that which is 4D 00448. It's at the very end of the bundle of hard copied documents. If you could have that 4D 00448. Let us know when you have it, Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see it's a much shorter document, but the name is Arif Pasalic. You know who he was. He was on the -- the Bosnia-Herzegovina army side. You're nodding. 18th of April also. In the spirit of the conclusions of the agreement, Izetbegovic, Boban immediately stop with the offensive activities, send report immediately. So with admirable succinctness, there's no doubt it's essentially the same thrust as the other document, Mr. Petkovic's document. You were familiar with these documents, were you, soon after your arrival or at least the agreement and the orders which they contained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember having seen a copy of the signed agreement. I think it was the -- it was signed on the 18th of April. But I don't remember having seen the specific orders as concerns each of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on then, please. The next document would be P 01988. If you could have that. That's also in the bundle of hard copy documents. And this is -- do you have that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you for being so quick. That's most helpful. The second page shows four signatures, Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Petkovic, both of whom are familiar names, and similarly Morillon, General Morillon, and Mr. Thebault, who was the European Community Monitoring Mission representative. And going back to the beginning of the document, 20th of April, during their common meeting held in Zenica and co-chaired by General Morillon and Mr. Thebault, I'm going quickly through this, number 1, BiH army and HVO are both legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are treated equally. Now, do you -- first of all, did you participate in any discussion relating to this meeting, this agreement that emerged? It was very shortly after you arrived, of course, but did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the drafting of this document, no, I did not participate, but I do seem to recall that a copy of this document arrived at Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In any case, you were familiar with the point number 1, were you, that it had been agreed that both the BiH army and the HVO were legal military forces and were to be treated equally? You knew that concept and that agreement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew of that concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And point 4 in the same document: "The commanders-in-chief will meet each week in order to ensure a close and permanent cooperation on all the subjects. Such meetings will be organised," it should be alternately would be the right English word, "in Mostar and Zenica. Next meeting will take place in Mostar." And those commanders-in-chief, that referred to Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Halilovic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they did in fact meet really, very frequently, didn't they, over the next few weeks and months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And sometimes you were present, and quite often you weren't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In most of the meetings I was present, but not in any of these meetings was I the representative of the Spanish Battalion. Rather, my task was a complementary one to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You made that very fairly clearly yesterday, Witness. This is correct, isn't it, in those high level meetings, you had a secondary role? Sometimes in the more local meetings of course you were the leader, the word used in translation was "spearheaded." That's your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next document I would like to show you then is P 02088. That's in the hard copy bundle as well. Let me know what you have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is a document which bears three signatures, Mr. Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, and described as witnessed by Dr. Tudjman. And we note -- and it's been mentioned that, although it's been dated April the 25th, it's actually at quarter to 1.00 in the morning. So it came at the end of an evening meeting, no doubt a long one, on the 24th. That -- the document begins, "Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, at a meeting in Zagreb," I'm skipping unnecessary words, "on April 24th by co-chairmen of the international conference, Lord Owen, Dr. Tudjman," in the presence of a lot of other, in many cases, extremely distinguished people and down to -- well, down to -- only down on the page to General Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic's name we see. Were you there at that meeting? I think you weren't, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you -- did you ever see a copy of this -- first of all, did you see a copy of this document in April or early May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In this meeting I was not present. To start with, I think the meeting was held in Zagreb, and I was not there, and I doubt that a representative of the Spanish Battalion was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you're quite right. It was recorded as being in Zagreb. And do you see item 4, the signatories of the joint statement reaffirm that the conflicts between units of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina are contrary -- in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, are contrary to the representatives of the two peoples? You see that, first of all, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... signatories of the joint statement condemn most severely all violations of the rules of international humanitarian law regardless of their perpetrators, both sides having been responsible according to data available so far. You see that as well, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From your -- now, it may have taken you a little while from April 25th to form your own assessment, but as you formed your own assessment and as you became familiar, does that summary there, does that represent your assessment of what had been happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does -- well, does that summary there, that both sides were responsible for violations and they were -- both sides were accepting that both sides were responsible, does that reflect your assessment as you came to be familiar and knowledgeable about what had been happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my personal opinion, which was formed over the six months or just over six months that I was in the area, if you would like a summary, I could say that I think there were no goodies and baddies, and that everybody to a greater or lesser extent was just as guilty as innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you're -- you're -- in that summary -- nevertheless, yesterday, you did say, and this remains your position, does it, that the higher-level people with whom you dealt did appear to show a genuine will to achieve peace and can we take it also to restrain and prevent the sort of excesses that are mentioned here? Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I reiterate what has been stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And among those people, because I've used the more general phrase higher-level people that appear to show that general will, do we and can we include Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must state that from my personal point of view, out of the people that I worked with, in the meetings in which the Croatian Defence Council was represented by Mr. Petkovic, we got the impression that there was a general positive will and predisposition to implementing and completing these agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask. I'm sorry to keep troubling you on this, but how much longer I have because I've got to make sure I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please tell me how much time was used up? You seem to have very complicated calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I hope, Your Honour. I did ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have already exceeded your time by six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you've nothing left, not even six minutes, because you've already used up one hour, six minutes. So normally you should be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm hearing I hope a slight hint that Your Honour might just give me two or three minutes just to rounds off these documents. It's been exceptionally difficult to calculate in the course of this afternoon's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we give counsel another two minutes? By exceptional approval, you have another 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll say thank you and move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, would you look at 4D00456 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, two minutes, not 10. The court reporter or the interpreter is too generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That bit doesn't count, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 4D 00456. Do you see that? I hope you do quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and that's signed by Mr. Boban. That's 10th of May, and it's -- it's a cease-fire command. Did you -- were you familiar with that at the time, and did you know that there was an equivalent order issued by Mr. Izetbegovic on the same date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had not seen that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And last document. I promise. P 02352. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 02352. 12th of May. Last page shows it signed by Mr. President Halilovic, Mr. Petkovic, and witnessed by General Morillon, Mr. Thebault. Was that a document with which you were familiar at the time? It was reconfirming their will to establish peace within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I have to take it as read given the time constraints. Is that a document you were familiar with at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hmm. Yes. I think I received a copy of this document in our headquarters in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, exceptional thanks for that exceptional indulgence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just one question of military order. You have been shown documents.
